items.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002
items.q: Monk then proceeded to sign with Riverside... it was the beginning of my career as a jazz record producer... I gained tremendously from the initially very frightening fact that this was the first artist of any significance who I worked with.

ctx.x: Right. Well I have to congratulate you on the contribution you’ve made to the art form called jazz. It’s really quite amazing the things you’ve been involved in and the careers that you have helped.

Well I must admit that I look back on it with a good deal of satisfaction. I’ve been very fortunate because in this business in particular, a lot of the associations that you form, at least initially, are accidental as hell. If someone tells me that I have been helpful to this or that career that’s exactly the thing that I want to hear because I have always looked on the role of the producer in a very specific way. Now one of the hardest things, and I’ve been at it, I’m getting perilously close to my fiftieth…

with doing this. The only real serious variation is that I have — I used to say in recent years — but for a lot of years, a lot of my attention has been focused on reissues and obviously the procedures are a little different there. For the most part that makes it possible to get into cliches like well I spent the whole day in the studio with Louis Armstrong or Duke Ellington or Fats Waller, and he didn’t give me a hard time. But that joke got busted about a year ago because one of my most recent reissue projects…

items.title: Orrin Keepnews — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Monk was our first significant artist at Riverside... Monk came about because... You wrote a review about him... Monk, we know the story of how Monk came into the plan. The first breakthrough record for Monk on Riverside was “Brilliant Cornish.”

ctx.x: We’re no strangers and so this is, for quite a joy, and a privilege. We’ve done several projects together, well let me just say we’ve done a few projects together, of which I’m very proud. Again, its an honor to be able to conduct this interview with you, to be able to share this time with you so that you could help the listening audience, and the historians, understand—further understand your contribution to this music since our last interview, which was in 1997. You did—you were a recipient—you are a recipient…

Well sometimes it’s hard for me to figure out what Orrin Keepnews has been doing. (Laughs) One of the things that I’ve done which, at the moment, is questionable in my mind as to whether it was a wise thing to be doing, but I have…All through my career I keep making noises about the importance to me of remaining as unaffiliated as possible. Actually, what had happened a few years before my previous interview, was that I had voluntarily, this is something you can’t imagine in the current situation, I voluntarily…

many years, so that in the year of 1980, which now sounds like a hell of a long time ago, and actually it was. What happened there was I left Fantasy and, as they say, it’s something that seems incredible and impossible in today’s world, but I voluntarily left. I was all the things that you want to get to be, I was running the new jazz program there and heavily involved in re-issue work. You know, it’s hard for me, even the language that I use then is hard to use again in absolutely today’s world. I made…
